patient.title: Topotecan by infusion · small-cell lung cancer
patient.purpose: This treatment aims to slow or shrink small-cell lung cancer that has returned after treatment, when repeating the first treatment is not appropriate. Benefit varies; your team explains the aim for you.

agents.name: Topotecan infusion
agents.explanation: Topotecan blocks topoisomerase I, an enzyme that relieves strain while DNA is copied. Unrepaired DNA breaks can stop dividing cancer cells; healthy blood-forming and gut cells can also be affected.
agents.watch: Call oncology immediately for fever or suddenly feeling unwell, unusual bleeding, severe tummy pain, persistent vomiting or diarrhoea, or new cough or breathlessness. Do not wait for the next cycle.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and mouth soreness
Rare severe bowel inflammation or perforation

patient.administration_text: Each infusion takes about 30 minutes. Blood review, preparation and observation add to appointment time. The consultant may prescribe only 3 or 4 treatment days in selected circumstances; follow the confirmed appointment plan.

support.text: Do not double a missed dose or take replacement capsules after vomiting without team advice. Record what happened, contact the oncology pharmacist/team, and follow the next scheduled dose in the agreed plan.

chapters.title: My treatment
chapters.intro: This treatment aims to slow or shrink extensive small-cell lung cancer when intravenous or combination chemotherapy is unsuitable. Benefit varies; your team explains the aim for you.

items.title: How it works
items.text: Etoposide interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme involved in DNA structure and repair. DNA damage can stop cancer cells dividing. Healthy blood-forming and other cells can also be affected. Absorption by mouth varies, so oral and intravenous doses are not interchangeable.

items.title: Evidence and limits
items.text: Older studies reported tumour responses with oral etoposide. The evidence is limited, and the different oral schedules cannot be assumed to have the same benefit or risks. A small uncontrolled study of a 21-day oral course does not establish a survival advantage or validate all three NCCP schedules. Its participants had recurrent cancer and substantial treatment toxicity; do not transfer its response percentage to an individual.

items.title: Missed or vomited capsules
items.text: Do not double a missed dose or take replacement capsules after vomiting without team advice. Record what happened, contact the oncology pharmacist/team, and follow the next scheduled dose in the agreed plan.

items.title: Safe handling
items.text: Take etoposide capsules on an empty stomach using the exact prescribed dose and days. Do not open, chew or crush them. Capsule strengths, quantities and storage follow the supplied pharmacy label. Oral and intravenous doses are not interchangeable. Keep away from children; ask the pharmacy how to return unused or damaged capsules.

chapters.title: When to call

patient.title: Carboplatin + Oral Etoposide
patient.purpose: This chemotherapy combination aims to control extensive-disease small-cell lung cancer, ease symptoms and help people live longer. Expected benefit depends on the cancer, general health and treatment choices. Ask what the team hopes it will achieve for you.

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop cancer cells dividing, but healthy tissues may also be affected. The dose is tailored using kidney function because the kidneys clear carboplatin.
agents.watch: Report ringing in the ears, hearing changes, numbness or loss of function. Report infection or unusual bruising/bleeding promptly and describe any symptoms during the infusion.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Hearing changes or tinnitus, which can persist
Numbness or tingling, which can persist

agents.name: Oral etoposide
agents.mechanism: Interferes with DNA repair and cell division
agents.explanation: Etoposide interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme involved in DNA structure and repair. DNA damage can stop cancer cells dividing. Healthy blood-forming and other cells can also be affected. Absorption by mouth varies, so oral and intravenous doses are not interchangeable.
agents.watch: Follow the exact capsule schedule and record doses. Report missed/vomited doses, infection, bruising, mouth ulcers or severe bowel symptoms. Do not double or convert doses yourself.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding

patient.schedule_summary: Carboplatin is planned into a vein on Day 1, before oral etoposide. Etoposide capsules are prescribed twice daily on Days 1, 2 and 3 only, on an empty stomach. The cycle repeats every 21 days while treatment is helping and side effects remain acceptable. Your team decides when to delay, change or stop; the source does not set a fixed number of cycles.
patient.administration_text: Carboplatin runs into a vein over about 30 minutes on Day 1. Etoposide is taken as capsules by mouth twice daily on Days 1–3, with the Day 1 sequence confirmed by the unit. The visit includes blood-result review, prevention medicines, preparation and observation. The pharmacy label gives your exact capsule strengths, number and times; do not calculate capsules from this guide.

patient.timeline_note: This shows one planned cycle. It does not predict when symptoms will occur or guarantee safe days. Use the prescribed calendar and team instructions if dates change.
patient.safety_note: Illness can be serious at any point in the cycle. Follow the unit’s temperature threshold and emergency instructions; call for shaking chills or sudden illness even without a high temperature.
patient.urgent_extra: Call your unit urgently for fever at its stated threshold, shaking chills, sudden illness, new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, unusual or uncontrolled bleeding, severe diarrhoea, repeated vomiting, inability to drink, very little urine, or a spreading/blistering rash. Swelling of the tongue/throat or trouble breathing can be an emergency. Report new tinnitus, hearing change, numbness or difficulty walking promptly.
patient.teachback: Can you describe which medicine is given through a drip, which capsules you take twice daily on Days 1–3, what to do if a dose is missed or vomited, and whom to contact urgently?
patient.consent_support: Discuss the individual treatment aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting hearing/nerve/kidney effects, fertility and pregnancy advice, safe capsule use, practical support and the possibility of dose delays or changes. Oral treatment is chemotherapy and needs the same careful safety review as an infusion.

day_groups.body: Attend the blood tests requested by the team. Low counts, fatigue and mouth or bowel problems may develop between visits. Hearing and nerve symptoms can build across cycles.
day_groups.action: Use the emergency contact plan at any time; do not wait for the next infusion.

day_groups.title: Review before another cycle
day_groups.body: The team checks blood counts, kidney/liver results, symptoms and treatment benefit before authorising another cycle.
day_groups.action: Do not start the next capsule course until your team confirms it. Bring the medicine list and dose record.

support.title: Your capsule prescription
support.text: Follow the prescribed capsule count and twice-daily Days 1–3 schedule exactly, using the written calendar to record each dose. Take capsules on an empty stomach with water; ask the pharmacist to explain the timing around food. Do not chew, open or crush capsules. If swallowing is difficult, contact the team before taking them; do not substitute an intravenous preparation or change the dose yourself.

support.title: Missed or vomited doses
support.text: If a dose is missed, do not double the next dose or extend the course. The manufacturer leaflet advises taking the next dose when due; inform your oncology pharmacist/team and follow your written plan. If you vomit after a dose, contact the team for instructions rather than automatically taking replacement capsules. BC Cancer specifically advises no repeat dose after vomiting within one hour unless the healthcare team directs it. Persistent vomiting or inability to keep fluids down needs urgent advice.

support.title: Safe handling and storage
support.text: Keep capsules in their original pack, away from children and excess heat or damp, following the supplied label. The manufacturer leaflet advises gloves for handling and washing hands afterwards. Do not open a blister with a leaking capsule; ask the pharmacist what to do. Return unused capsules through the pharmacy; do not put them in household waste or drains.

support.title: Sickness prevention across several days
support.text: Carboplatin Day 1 has high sickness risk; the oral etoposide-only days have a different risk. Your team provides one clear prevention and rescue plan covering treatment days and the next two days. Some medicines overlap; take only the reconciled prescription and do not repeat the full Day 1 plan on your own.

support.title: Fluids and symptom reporting
support.text: Ask for a drinking plan appropriate to your heart and kidney health. Report inability to drink or reduced urine promptly. Keep mouth-care advice and the emergency number nearby.

support.title: Other medicines and vaccines
support.text: Show the team all prescribed and non-prescribed medicines, supplements and vaccines. Etoposide has important interactions. Check before adding or stopping medicines; ask about contraception and fertility before treatment.

chapters.title: Why this treatment is being offered
chapters.intro: Start with the individual aim and the exact prescription.

items.title: The treatment aim
items.text: This chemotherapy combination aims to control extensive-disease small-cell lung cancer, ease symptoms and help people live longer. Expected benefit depends on the cancer, general health and treatment choices. Ask what the team hopes it will achieve for you.

items.title: The precise regimen
items.text: This guide covers carboplatin plus oral etoposide for extensive-disease small-cell lung cancer in people unsuitable for cisplatin-based treatment. It does not cover an intravenous etoposide schedule or an added immunotherapy medicine. If the prescription differs, ask for its matching guide and consent discussion.

items.title: What the evidence can tell us
items.text: The studies cited by NCCP support platinum–etoposide treatment and provide background on using etoposide by mouth, but they did not test this exact carboplatin plus all-oral three-day schedule. The oral comparison used cisplatin and a mixture of intravenous and oral etoposide. A separate pooled analysis compared platinum choices across several trials. These results cannot give a precise survival estimate for this prescription or predict your individual benefit.

chapters.title: Preparing for the first cycle
chapters.intro: Bring concerns about medicines, swallowing, memory or home support to the team.

items.title: Baseline checks
items.text: Blood, kidney and liver tests are needed before treatment. Kidney measurements help set carboplatin dosing; hearing tests may be arranged if needed. Tell the team about existing hearing or nerve problems.

items.title: Practice the capsule plan

If swallowing is difficult, contact the team before taking them; do not substitute an intravenous preparation or change the dose yourself.

items.title: Fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation, contraception and any pregnancy plans before starting. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are excluded in this regimen. Your team explains the medicine-specific contraception period.

chapters.title: Taking chemotherapy at home
chapters.intro: An oral medicine still requires careful treatment checks.

chapters.title: What to watch for
chapters.intro: Tell the team early so symptoms can be assessed and treated.

items.title: Blood counts and infection
items.text: Both medicines can lower blood counts, increasing infection, bleeding or anaemia risk. Attend monitoring and report sudden illness, bruising or bleeding.

items.title: Mouth, stomach and energy
items.text: Sickness, diarrhoea, constipation, mouth soreness, appetite loss, fatigue and hair loss may occur. Ask for help early; inability to drink or persistent vomiting needs urgent advice.

items.title: Hearing, nerves and kidneys
items.text: Tell the team about tinnitus, hearing change, numbness, weakness, balance problems or reduced urine. Some effects can persist after treatment.

items.title: Less common serious effects
items.text: Serious allergic or skin reactions can occur. Etoposide also carries a risk of secondary leukaemia; ask the team to explain serious and lasting risks in your situation.

chapters.title: When to get urgent help
chapters.intro: Use the unit’s 24-hour number and emergency instructions.

items.title: Urgent symptoms
items.text: Call your unit urgently for fever at its stated threshold, shaking chills, sudden illness, new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, unusual or uncontrolled bleeding, severe diarrhoea, repeated vomiting, inability to drink, very little urine, or a spreading/blistering rash. Swelling of the tongue/throat or trouble breathing can be an emergency. Report new tinnitus, hearing change, numbness or difficulty walking promptly.

items.title: What to say when you call
items.text: Give the regimen name, last infusion and capsule dose, symptoms and when they began. Explain whether you can drink and pass urine. Do not delay calling to collect all the details.

chapters.title: Reviewing the course and next steps
chapters.intro: The number of cycles is a clinical decision.

items.title: Before another cycle
items.text: Attend weekly blood counts as arranged and kidney/liver tests before each cycle. The team reviews toxicity and benefit; do not restart capsules until authorised.

items.title: How long treatment continues
items.text: Carboplatin is planned into a vein on Day 1, before oral etoposide. Etoposide capsules are prescribed twice daily on Days 1, 2 and 3 only, on an empty stomach. The cycle repeats every 21 days while treatment is helping and side effects remain acceptable. Your team decides when to delay, change or stop; the source does not set a fixed number of cycles.

items.title: After a change or stop
items.text: Confirm which medicines stop or continue, how unused capsules are returned, and follow-up for ongoing symptoms. Ask who will contact you about the next treatment or supportive-care plan.

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

questions.q: Are oral capsules a weaker form of chemotherapy?
questions.a: No. Etoposide capsules are chemotherapy and can cause serious effects. Their absorption differs from an infusion, so only the treating team can choose or change the dose.

questions.q: What if I miss or vomit a dose?
questions.a: If a dose is missed, do not double the next dose or extend the course. The manufacturer leaflet advises taking the next dose when due; inform your oncology pharmacist/team and follow your written plan. If you vomit after a dose, contact the team for instructions rather than automatically taking replacement capsules. BC Cancer specifically advises no repeat dose after vomiting within one hour unless the healthcare team directs it. Persistent vomiting or inability to keep fluids down needs urgent advice.

questions.q: Do I continue capsules every day until the next infusion?
questions.a: No. This regimen prescribes twice-daily etoposide on Days 1–3 only. Use your own written calendar and wait for the team to confirm the next cycle.

questions.q: Will I always have a fixed number of cycles?
questions.a: The current NCCP source continues this regimen until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity, with ongoing review. Your team agrees the number of cycles and may stop or change earlier.

patient.title: Carboplatin and vinorelbine · lung cancer
patient.purpose: This chemotherapy aims to control lung cancer and symptoms when cisplatin is unsuitable. The team reviews benefit, side effects and your priorities.

agents.name: Vinorelbine
agents.mechanism: Disrupts microtubules needed for cell division
agents.explanation: Vinorelbine disrupts the cell structures that help divide chromosomes. This can slow cancer growth and also affect blood cells, nerves and the bowel.
agents.watch: Report fever, constipation, numbness or pain at the infusion site promptly.
risks: Low blood counts and serious infection

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin forms links in DNA that hinder copying and repair. Healthy tissues can also be harmed. Its dose depends on target exposure (AUC) and measured or estimated kidney function; AUC is not a fixed number of milligrams. There are two planned doses in this regimen.
agents.watch: Report fever, bleeding, nausea, hearing changes or numbness. Tell the nurse immediately about possible allergy during the infusion.

phases.label: Four 21 day cycles
phases.detail: Four 21 day cycles are planned, unless treatment stops or changes earlier. Day 1: carboplatin plus vinorelbine. Day 8: vinorelbine only. Your prescription specifies vinorelbine by drip OR capsules; these are alternatives, not extra doses.

phases.label: Review after treatment
phases.detail: Four cycles take about 12 weeks without delays. Your team agrees response scans and what happens next. Surgery or radiotherapy is not automatically included.

timeline.text: Symptoms may occur on any day; this is not a personal risk curve.

support.text: Day 1 carboplatin needs a stronger anti-sickness plan. Day 8 depends on whether vinorelbine is by drip or capsules. Use the written prescription for that day and route; do not repeat the entire Day 1course automatically.

support.title: Bowel plan
support.text: Vinorelbine and some anti-sickness medicines can cause constipation. Follow the prescribed bowel plan and call for severe tummy pain, swelling or vomiting.

support.title: If capsules are prescribed
support.text: Swallow whole with water and some food. Do not chew or open capsules. Do not take an extra dose after vomiting; contact the team for missed-dose advice. Return damaged capsules to pharmacy.

support.title: Check medicine interactions
support.text: The team should check all medicines, including anti-sickness treatment. Do not start new tablets, supplements or vaccines without advice.

questions.q: Am I having both oral and IV vinorelbine?
questions.a: No. Your written plan must identify the prescribed route for each dose. Do not treat capsule instructions as additional treatment.

questions.q: Why is Day 8different?
questions.a: Only vinorelbine is planned. Blood results, symptoms and the route determine whether dosing and the support plan are appropriate.

questions.q: What if treatment changes?
questions.a: Ask your team to update the cycle record, prescription and contact plan. A stamp is not permission for the next dose.

agents.name: Vinorelbine
agents.mechanism: Disrupts the machinery of cell division
agents.explanation: Vinorelbine disrupts the tiny structures a cell needs to divide. This can stop cancer cells multiplying. Healthy blood-forming cells, gut cells and nerves can also be affected.
agents.watch: Use the treating unit’s 24-hour emergency number and local fever threshold. Contact immediately for fever/chills, sudden illness, breathlessness/chest pain, uncontrolled vomiting, severe abdominal pain/obstruction symptoms, bleeding or severe allergy. Do not wait until the next visit.

Nerve effects and uncommon lung/heart toxicity

questions.q: Can IV and oral vinorelbine be exchanged?
questions.a: For IV use only; intrathecal administration may be fatal. Oral and IV vinorelbine are not interchangeable mg-for-mg. Stop infusion and tell staff immediately about pain, burning, swelling or leakage at the IV site; extravasation can damage tissue.

questions.q: How long will treatment continue?
questions.a: Repeated 21-day cycles until progression/unacceptable toxicity; team review determines continuation.

questions.q: Do I need regular heart scans?
questions.a: Review cardiovascular history and new symptoms. These monotherapy NCCP protocols do not mandate the serial LVEF/echo schedule used for anthracyclines or trastuzumab; arrange cardiac tests when clinically indicated.

questions.q: How long is an infusion visit?
questions.a: The source describes a short infusion followed by a saline flush. Your unit confirms the product-specific infusion instructions and complete visit length, including blood results, preparation and observation.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: Studies support vinorelbine as an option in selected people with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer. The strength and type of evidence differ for the IV and capsule schedules.
evidence.population: Non-small-cell lung cancer; the cited study enrolled older adults with advanced disease.
evidence.interpretation: The team considers tumour tests, previous treatment, health, symptoms and your preferences. Results from a group cannot predict your own benefit.
evidence.limitations: Historical studies do not establish superiority over current biomarker-directed or immunotherapy options. Oral and IV study results are not interchangeable.

anatomy: Low blood counts can cause infection, tiredness, bruising or bleeding. Fever, chills or sudden illness: call oncology immediately.
Constipation, vomiting or sore mouth can occur. Severe pain, swelling, repeated vomiting or no stool/gas: urgent assessment; do not take extra laxatives.
Nerve effects may change sensation, grip, walking or bowel movement. Report changes early because the next dose may need to wait or be reduced.
Tiredness, hair thinning/loss and liver-test changes can occur. Pace activities and tell the team if eating, drinking or daily tasks become difficult.
New chest pain, sudden or worsening breathlessness, or severe allergic symptoms need urgent medical help. Previous heart disease and interacting medicines need review before treatment.
Tell staff immediately about burning, pain, swelling or leakage.

questions.q: Can IV and oral vinorelbine be exchanged?
questions.a: For IV use only; intrathecal administration may be fatal. Oral and IV vinorelbine are not interchangeable mg-for-mg. Stop infusion and tell staff immediately about pain, burning, swelling or leakage at the IV site; extravasation can damage tissue.

questions.q: How long will treatment continue?
questions.a: Repeated 21-day cycles until progression/unacceptable toxicity; team review determines continuation.

questions.q: Do I need regular heart scans?
questions.a: Review cardiovascular history and new symptoms. These monotherapy NCCP protocols do not mandate the serial LVEF/echo schedule used for anthracyclines or trastuzumab; arrange cardiac tests when clinically indicated.

questions.q: How long is an infusion visit?
questions.a: The source describes a short infusion followed by a saline flush. Your unit confirms the product-specific infusion instructions and complete visit length, including blood results, preparation and observation.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: Studies support vinorelbine as an option in selected people with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer. The strength and type of evidence differ for the IV and capsule schedules.
evidence.population: Non-small-cell lung cancer; the cited study enrolled older adults with advanced disease.
evidence.interpretation: The team considers tumour tests, previous treatment, health, symptoms and your preferences. Results from a group cannot predict your own benefit.
evidence.limitations: Historical studies do not establish superiority over current biomarker-directed or immunotherapy options. Oral and IV study results are not interchangeable.

anatomy: Low blood counts can cause infection, tiredness, bruising or bleeding. Fever, chills or sudden illness: call oncology immediately.
Constipation, vomiting or sore mouth can occur. Severe pain, swelling, repeated vomiting or no stool/gas: urgent assessment; do not take extra laxatives.
Nerve effects may change sensation, grip, walking or bowel movement. Report changes early because the next dose may need to wait or be reduced.
Tiredness, hair thinning/loss and liver-test changes can occur. Pace activities and tell the team if eating, drinking or daily tasks become difficult.
New chest pain, sudden or worsening breathlessness, or severe allergic symptoms need urgent medical help. Previous heart disease and interacting medicines need review before treatment.
Tell staff immediately about burning, pain, swelling or leakage.

support.title: Sickness plan
support.text: Take the anti-sickness medicine exactly as prescribed before/around the weekly capsule dose; contact the team if it is not controlling symptoms.

support.title: Bowel care
support.text: Agree a constipation plan, particularly if using opioids or ondansetron. Severe abdominal pain, swelling, repeated vomiting or inability to pass stool/gas needs urgent assessment; do not simply add laxatives.

support.title: Medicines and vaccines
support.text: Check every new prescription, supplement and vaccine with the team; avoid grapefruit. Live vaccines and interacting medicines need review.

support.title: Weekly safety
support.text: Take capsules only once weekly after the team clears the blood results. Do not repeat a vomited dose or increase the capsules yourself.

questions.q: Can IV and oral vinorelbine be exchanged?
questions.a: Oral 60/80 mg/m² and IV 25/30 mg/m² have pharmacokinetic equivalence references, but never convertmg-for-mg or swap routes yourself. Dose rules and schedules differ.

questions.q: How long will treatment continue?
questions.a: Continue weekly while helpful and tolerated; no fixed total number of weeks.

questions.q: Do I need regular heart scans?
questions.a: Review cardiovascular history and new symptoms. These monotherapy NCCP protocols do not mandate the serial LVEF/echo schedule used for anthracyclines or trastuzumab; arrange cardiac tests when clinically indicated.

questions.q: What if I vomit, miss a dose or find damaged capsules?
questions.a: Do not take another dose if vomiting occurs within a few hours. Contact the team and record the dose taken. Do not swallow damaged capsules. Return them to pharmacy; immediately wash any contact with contents using water or saline. Missed/late dose: contact the team for the next date. Do not double or move the weekly schedule yourself. This is pragmatic medication-safety advice, not an extra NCCP catch-up schedule.

questions.q: How do I store the capsules?
questions.a: Current Vinorelbine Accord SmPC: refrigerator 2–8°C. Confirm the dispensed brand/pack instructions; keep in original packaging and out of children’s reach. Return unused or damaged capsules to pharmacy; follow cytotoxic handling advice.

questions.q: Does dose four always use more capsules?
questions.a: No. The team reviews the lowest counts and side effects after the first three doses. Take only the current prescribed dose; severe or repeated low counts can prevent an increase.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: Studies support vinorelbine as an option in selected people with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer. The strength and type of evidence differ for the IV and capsule schedules.
evidence.population: Non-small-cell lung cancer; the cited study enrolled older adults with advanced disease.
evidence.interpretation: The team considers tumour tests, previous treatment, health, symptoms and your preferences. Results from a group cannot predict your own benefit.
evidence.limitations: Historical studies do not establish superiority over current biomarker-directed or immunotherapy options. Oral and IV study results are not interchangeable.

anatomy: Low blood counts can cause infection, tiredness, bruising or bleeding. Fever, chills or sudden illness: call oncology immediately.

evidence.population: 56 chemotherapy-naive older adults with advanced NSCLC enrolled April 2001–March 2002.
evidence.comparison: Single-arm phase II; no randomised comparator.
evidence.applicability: 60 mg/m² once weekly for the first three administrations, then 80 mg/m² if tolerated: matches the NCCP escalation framework.

endpoints.result_text: 6 of 56 participants (11%) had a partial response; 25 had stable disease.
endpoints.interpretation: Descriptive activity estimate; it cannot show comparative survival benefit.

evidence.qualitative_result: The historical single-arm study found antitumour activity with weekly oral treatment. A 2025 pooled analysis of 247 participants from four phase II weekly-treatment arms also describes activity, but has no pooled concurrent control and includes historical treatment-naive populations. Its April 2026 correction clarifies dose-escalation and response denominators and event-estimate footnotes.
limitations: Small older-adult, treatment-naive population; no randomised comparison, no proof of equivalence to IV vinorelbine or superiority over modern options. Do not borrow ELVIS IV survival effects.
The 2025 pooled reanalysis combines studies conducted before routine immunotherapy; it is not a randomised comparison against modern options. Sponsor-funded; the 2026 correction was checked.

support.title: Bowel care

questions.q: Can IV and oral vinorelbine be exchanged?
questions.a: Oral 60/80 mg/m² and IV 25/30 mg/m² have pharmacokinetic equivalence references, but never convertmg-for-mg or swap routes yourself. Dose rules and schedules differ.

questions.q: How long will treatment continue?
questions.a: Continue weekly while helpful and tolerated; no fixed total number of weeks.

questions.q: Do I need regular heart scans?
questions.a: Review cardiovascular history and new symptoms. These monotherapy NCCP protocols do not mandate the serial LVEF/echo schedule used for anthracyclines or trastuzumab; arrange cardiac tests when clinically indicated.

questions.q: What if I vomit, miss a dose or find damaged capsules?
questions.a: Do not take another dose if vomiting occurs within a few hours. Contact the team and record the dose taken. Do not swallow damaged capsules. Return them to pharmacy; immediately wash any contact with contents using water or saline. Missed/late dose: contact the team for the next date. Do not double or move the weekly schedule yourself. This is pragmatic medication-safety advice, not an extra NCCP catch-up schedule.

questions.q: How do I store the capsules?
questions.a: Current Vinorelbine Accord SmPC: refrigerator 2–8°C. Confirm the dispensed brand/pack instructions; keep in original packaging and out of children’s reach. Return unused or damaged capsules to pharmacy; follow cytotoxic handling advice.

questions.q: Does dose four always use more capsules?
questions.a: No. The team reviews the lowest counts and side effects after the first three doses. Take only the current prescribed dose; severe or repeated low counts can prevent an increase.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: Studies support vinorelbine as an option in selected people with advanced non-small-cell lung cancer. The strength and type of evidence differ for the IV and capsule schedules.
evidence.population: Non-small-cell lung cancer; the cited study enrolled older adults with advanced disease.
evidence.interpretation: The team considers tumour tests, previous treatment, health, symptoms and your preferences. Results from a group cannot predict your own benefit.
evidence.limitations: Historical studies do not establish superiority over current biomarker-directed or immunotherapy options. Oral and IV study results are not interchangeable.

details.text: Take with some food; swallow capsules whole with water. Do not chew, suck or dissolve. anatomy: Low blood counts can cause infection, tiredness, bruising or bleeding. Fever, chills or sudden illness: call oncology immediately.
Constipation, vomiting or sore mouth can occur. Severe pain, swelling, repeated vomiting or no stool/gas: urgent assessment; do not take extra laxatives.
Nerve effects may change sensation, grip, walking or bowel movement. Report changes early because the next dose may need to wait or be reduced.
Tiredness, hair thinning/loss and liver-test changes can occur. Pace activities and tell the team if eating, drinking or daily tasks become difficult.
New chest pain, sudden or worsening breathlessness, or severe allergic symptoms need urgent medical help. Previous heart disease and interacting medicines need review before treatment.

evidence.applicability: 60 mg/m² once weekly for the first three administrations, then 80 mg/m² if tolerated: matches the NCCP escalation framework.

endpoints.result_text: 6 of 56 participants (11%) had a partial response; 25 had stable disease.
endpoints.interpretation: Descriptive activity estimate; it cannot show comparative survival benefit.

sources.label: Gridelli et al., European Journal of Cancer 2004: weekly oral vinorelbine in older adults with advanced NSCLC

evidence.qualitative_result: The historical single-arm study found antitumour activity with weekly oral treatment. A 2025 pooled analysis of 247 participants from four phase II weekly-treatment arms also describes activity, but has no pooled concurrent control and includes historical treatment-naive populations. Its April 2026 correction clarifies dose-escalation and response denominators and event-estimate footnotes.
limitations: Small older-adult, treatment-naive population; no randomised comparison, no proof of equivalence to IV vinorelbine or superiority over modern options. Do not borrow ELVIS IV survival effects.
The 2025 pooled reanalysis combines studies conducted before routine immunotherapy; it is not a randomised comparison against modern options. Sponsor-funded; the 2026 correction was checked.

support.title: Premedication
support.text: Take dexamethasone exactly as prescribed before and after docetaxel. Tell the unit about missed doses before infusion; any alternative needs the prescriber’s decision. Do not double a dose or add another steroid course yourself.

support.title: Nausea, bowel symptoms and pain
support.text: Use your individual anti-sickness and pain plan. Contact the team if symptoms are uncontrolled or you cannot drink. Antihistamines and other support medicines may cause drowsiness; arrange transport if advised.

support.title: Nerves and daily activities
support.text: Report tingling, numbness or weakness early, including effects on buttons, writing, walking or balance. Protect hands and feet and take care with hot surfaces if sensation changes.

support.title: Infection and blood counts
support.text: Each treatment needs its own blood and symptom review. A growth-factor injection may be prescribed after individual risk assessment; follow its separate instructions. Fever or sudden illness needs immediate contact on any day.

questions.q: What benefit is realistic for me and what other options are available?
questions.a: Treatment aims to slow or shrink lung cancer and relieve symptoms after previous chemotherapy. Expected benefit, side effects, other options and your priorities guide the decision. A historical randomised trial found that docetaxel 75 mg/m² every three weeks prolonged survival compared with supportive care alone in selected people whose NSCLC had progressed after platinum chemotherapy. Modern previous treatment and available alternatives differ, so the trial cannot predict an individual outcome.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: A historical randomised trial found that docetaxel 75 mg/m² every three weeks prolonged survival compared with supportive care alone in selected people whose NSCLC had progressed after platinum chemotherapy. Modern previous treatment and available alternatives differ, so the trial cannot predict an individual outcome.
evidence.population: NCCP 00203a: locally advanced or metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer after failure of prior chemotherapy. This is docetaxel alone; a platinum or other partner needs its own regimen.
evidence.interpretation: Discuss possible benefit, alternatives and uncertainty for your own situation. The treatment aim is cancer control and symptom relief.
evidence.limitations: TAX317 was a historical randomised study after platinum chemotherapy; it predates current targeted therapy and immunotherapy. The 75 mg/m² cohort followed an initial 100 mg/m² cohort; preserve the dose-specific comparison and do not combine them as one 75 mg/m² estimate. NCCP limits this NSCLC course to six cycles. Trial results are population averages, not an individual survival prediction. TAX320 compared docetaxel with vinorelbine/ifosfamide; its overall survival comparison did not reach statistical significance. Do not imply all comparators showed the same result.

support.title: Premedication
support.text: Take dexamethasone exactly as prescribed before and after docetaxel. Tell the unit about missed doses before infusion; any alternative needs the prescriber’s decision. Do not double a dose or add another steroid course yourself.

support.title: Nausea, bowel symptoms and pain
support.text: Use your individual anti-sickness and pain plan. Contact the team if symptoms are uncontrolled or you cannot drink. Antihistamines and other support medicines may cause drowsiness; arrange transport if advised.

support.title: Nerves and daily activities
support.text: Report tingling, numbness or weakness early, including effects on buttons, writing, walking or balance. Protect hands and feet and take care with hot surfaces if sensation changes.

support.title: Infection and blood counts
support.text: Each treatment needs its own blood and symptom review. A growth-factor injection may be prescribed after individual risk assessment; follow its separate instructions. Fever or sudden illness needs immediate contact on any day.

TAX320 compared docetaxel with vinorelbine/ifosfamide; its overall survival comparison did not reach statistical significance. Do not imply all comparators showed the same result.

patient.title: Pemetrexed Monotherapy

agents.name: Pemetrexed
agents.explanation: Pemetrexed blocks several enzymes that use folate to make the building blocks of DNA and RNA. This can slow or stop cancer-cell growth. Healthy cells can also be affected. Prescribed folic acid and vitamin B12 reduce important toxicities and are part of treatment.
agents.watch: Take the prescribed folic acid and attend for B12. Report mouth sores, diarrhoea, a rash, breathlessness or reduced urine; check before taking ibuprofen or other non-prescription medicines.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Skin rash; rarely serious skin reactions

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

questions.q: Is this the same as pemetrexed with pembrolizumab?
questions.a: This guide covers pemetrexed on its own for maintenance or second-line treatment of selected non-squamous non-small-cell lung cancer. If pembrolizumab or another immunotherapy is also prescribed, use the matching combination regimen and its additional consent, monitoring and urgent advice. Pemetrexed with pembrolizumab maintenance is a different treatment plan.

questions.q: What is maintenance treatment?
questions.a: Maintenance means continuing cancer treatment after the initial chemotherapy has finished and the cancer has not progressed. In this regimen pemetrexed is the only anti-cancer medicine. Your team confirms whether it is being continued from your earlier combination or started as a new maintenance medicine.

questions.q: How many cycles will I have?
questions.a: Treatment is planned every three weeks while it is helping and side effects remain acceptable. There is no fixed total number of cycles in this regimen. Scans, symptoms, blood results, your priorities and the oncology review guide continuation, delays, changes or stopping.

questions.q: Can I stop the vitamins when platinum treatment stops?
questions.a: Do not stop them because platinum stops. Folic acid and B12 protect against pemetrexed toxicity and continue according to the pemetrexed plan. The team checks your existing vitamin schedule at a phase change.

questions.q: How long will I be at the unit?
questions.a: Pemetrexed is infused into a vein over about 10 minutes on Day 1. The whole visit is longer because it includes blood-result review, symptom checks, medicines, preparation and observation. The team can use a cannula or suitable existing line; this regimen has no routine take-home infusion pump.

questions.q: Can I take my usual painkillers?
questions.a: Check with the team before using ibuprofen, other anti-inflammatory painkillers, aspirin or any new medicine. Kidney function and the medicine determine whether and when it needs interruption. Do not stop a prescribed medicine on your own; ask for a written plan.

questions.q: Can I have vaccinations while on treatment?
questions.a: Check first with the oncology team. Live vaccines, including yellow fever vaccine, can be unsafe during treatment. Other vaccines may still be appropriate; do not assume every vaccine should be stopped.

patient.phases_title: A three-week cycle within an ongoing treatment plan
patient.phases_note: Treatment is planned every three weeks while it is helping and side effects remain acceptable. There is no fixed total number of cycles in this regimen. Scans, symptoms, blood results, your priorities and the oncology review guide continuation, delays, changes or stopping.
patient.timeline_note: This reference cycle shows care and checks, not predicted safe or high-risk days. Symptoms can occur at any time.
patient.safety_note: Follow your unit’s emergency instructions and use its 24-hour number. Serious infection can occur without a high temperature; sudden illness or shivering still needs immediate advice.
patient.teachback: Can you explain whether this is maintenance or second-line treatment, which vitamin and steroid medicines continue, when B12 is due, and how to get urgent help?
patient.consent_support: Discuss whether this is maintenance or second-line treatment, the individual aim, likely benefit and uncertainty, alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious harms, possible lasting kidney or nerve effects, fertility and pregnancy, vitamin and steroid medicines, practical burdens and your right to reconsider. A discussion aid supports but does not replace informed consent.
patient.urgent_extra: Call your oncology 24-hour number immediately for a temperature of 37.5°C or above, 36°C or below, shivering or sudden illness. Call urgently for new breathlessness, chest pain, bleeding, severe or persistent diarrhoea, vomiting despite medicines, inability to drink, very little urine or a spreading or blistering rash. Do not wait for the next visit; serious infection can occur without a high temperature.

chapters.title: Understanding your treatment
chapters.intro: Confirm the treatment aim and the medicines on your prescription.

items.title: Maintenance or second-line
items.text: Pemetrexed is chemotherapy used to control selected non-squamous non-small-cell lung cancer that is locally advanced or has spread. Maintenance aims to keep cancer controlled after platinum chemotherapy has finished without the cancer progressing. Second-line treatment is a separate treatment decision after previous chemotherapy. Ask which aim and indication apply to you.

items.title: One medicine, its own plan
items.text: This guide covers pemetrexed on its own for maintenance or second-line treatment of selected non-squamous non-small-cell lung cancer. If pembrolizumab or another immunotherapy is also prescribed, use the matching combination regimen and its additional consent, monitoring and urgent advice. Pemetrexed with pembrolizumab maintenance is a different treatment plan.

items.title: Treatment length
items.text: Treatment is planned every three weeks while it is helping and side effects remain acceptable. There is no fixed total number of cycles in this regimen. Scans, symptoms, blood results, your priorities and the oncology review guide continuation, delays, changes or stopping.

chapters.title: Before starting or changing to maintenance
chapters.intro: A change in phase needs a clear new prescription and review.

items.title: Checks before the dose
items.text: Blood count, kidney and liver tests are checked before starting and before each cycle. Tell the team about infections, breathlessness, bowel or mouth problems, rash, numbness and any previous severe treatment reaction.

items.title: Confirm the vitamin schedule
items.text: Check how much folic acid you take and when your last B12 injection was given. If you already received pemetrexed, the team carries forward the correct vitamin schedule.

items.title: Medicines review
items.text: Check with the team before using ibuprofen, other anti-inflammatory painkillers, aspirin or any new medicine. Kidney function and the medicine determine whether and when it needs interruption. Do not stop a prescribed medicine on your own; ask for a written plan.

items.title: Your consent conversation
items.text: Discuss whether this is maintenance or second-line treatment, the individual aim, likely benefit and uncertainty, alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious harms, possible lasting kidney or nerve effects, fertility and pregnancy, vitamin and steroid medicines, practical burdens and your right to reconsider. A discussion aid supports but does not replace informed consent.

chapters.title: Treatment day
chapters.intro: Assessment comes before dose authorisation.

items.title: Your infusion
items.text: Pemetrexed is infused into a vein over about 10 minutes on Day 1. The whole visit is longer because it includes blood-result review, symptom checks, medicines, preparation and observation. The team can use a cannula or suitable existing line; this regimen has no routine take-home infusion pump.

items.title: Tell the nurse immediately
items.text: Report feeling unwell, itching, swelling, wheeze, chest tightness or pain, burning or redness around the drip.

items.title: A delay or dose change
items.text: The team may delay or reduce a dose so that blood counts or symptoms can recover. A change does not itself mean the treatment has failed; ask why it is needed and when review is planned.

chapters.title: Care between visits
chapters.intro: Keep a short symptom record and ask for help early.

items.title: Vitamins and steroids
items.text: Follow the written folic acid, B12, steroid and anti-sickness plan. Tell the team promptly about missed doses or vomiting that prevents you keeping medicines down.

items.title: Mouth, bowel and skin symptoms
items.text: Report mouth ulcers, difficulty eating or drinking, persistent diarrhoea, rash and changes in daily function. Severe symptoms or sudden illness need urgent advice.

items.title: Daily life and support
items.text: Balance activity with rest. Ask for help with fatigue, eating, transport, work, finances or emotional wellbeing. Discuss what matters most to you at each review.

items.title: Pregnancy, fertility and feeding
items.text: Tell the team immediately if pregnancy is possible. Discuss fertility preservation and contraception before treatment and confirm the medicine-specific duration after the final dose. Breastfeeding must stop during pemetrexed.

chapters.title: When to get urgent help
chapters.intro: Keep your oncology contact number available day and night.

items.title: Call immediately
items.text: Call your oncology 24-hour number immediately for a temperature of 37.5°C or above, 36°C or below, shivering or sudden illness. Call urgently for new breathlessness, chest pain, bleeding, severe or persistent diarrhoea, vomiting despite medicines, inability to drink, very little urine or a spreading or blistering rash. Do not wait for the next visit; serious infection can occur without a high temperature.

items.title: When you call
items.text: Give the medicine name, last treatment date and symptoms. Say whether you can drink, pass urine and manage everyday activities. Do not delay a call to collect these details.

items.title: Symptoms after stopping
items.text: New or worsening symptoms after the last dose still need advice. Explain that you recently had chemotherapy.

chapters.title: Review and the next plan
chapters.intro: Treatment decisions consider benefit, harms and your priorities.

items.title: Scans and disease review
items.text: Scans and other tests follow the Consultant treatment plan. There is no fixed scan interval in this regimen, and side effects do not reliably show whether treatment is working.

items.title: When treatment stops
items.text: Treatment is planned every three weeks while it is helping and side effects remain acceptable. There is no fixed total number of cycles in this regimen. Scans, symptoms, blood results, your priorities and the oncology review guide continuation, delays, changes or stopping.

items.title: After the final pemetrexed
items.text: Continue folic acid for 21 days after the last pemetrexed. Agree follow-up for persistent blood-count, kidney, nerve or other symptoms and confirm which support medicines stop.

chapters.title: Vaccines and radiotherapy
chapters.intro: Tell the team about planned vaccines and any past or planned radiotherapy.

items.title: Check before a vaccine
items.text: The team must review the vaccine type and timing. Yellow fever vaccine must not be given with pemetrexed; other live vaccines are also not usually suitable.

items.title: Past or planned radiotherapy
items.text: Tell the team, even if radiotherapy was years ago. Report new cough, breathlessness or a skin reaction in a previously treated area.

support.title: Folic acid every day
support.text: The source uses folic acid 350–1000 micrograms daily. Take at least five doses in the seven days before the first pemetrexed, continue throughout treatment and for 21 days after the final dose. Follow your own prescription and tell the team about missed doses.

support.title: Vitamin B12 injection
support.text: The source uses vitamin B12 1000 micrograms into a muscle during the week before the first pemetrexed, then every three cycles. Later injections may be on treatment day. A change from platinum treatment to maintenance does not automatically restart the B12 clock: your team checks the last dose and the next due date.

support.title: One steroid prescription
support.text: Pemetrexed rash prevention uses dexamethasone-equivalent 4 mg twice daily on the day before, day of and day after treatment. Your pharmacist or prescriber should give one clear steroid schedule that also accounts for any anti-sickness medicines. Do not add a second steroid course yourself.

support.title: Low-risk anti-sickness plan
support.text: Pemetrexed on its own has a low sickness risk. Take the prescribed prevention and rescue medicines and call if sickness persists. A previous platinum anti-sickness course should be reviewed when moving to pemetrexed alone.

support.title: Kidneys and other medicines
support.text: Check with the team before using ibuprofen, other anti-inflammatory painkillers, aspirin or any new medicine. Kidney function and the medicine determine whether and when it needs interruption. Do not stop a prescribed medicine on your own; ask for a written plan.

support.title: Reporting symptoms and getting help
support.text: Keep your 24-hour oncology number available, record symptoms and ask for practical or emotional support early.

support.title: Vaccines
support.text: Ask the oncology team before any vaccination. Some live vaccines are unsuitable during treatment; the team can advise on the right vaccine and timing.

evidence.title: Evidence depends on the treatment setting
evidence.intro: Maintenance and second-line studies answer different questions.
evidence.population: Selected advanced NSCLC populations after prior chemotherapy; the maintenance trials included patients without progression.
evidence.comparison_label: Placebo/supportive care in maintenance; docetaxel in second-line treatment
evidence.interpretation: Maintenance studies found longer disease control or survival with pemetrexed than placebo in selected patients whose cancer had not progressed after initial chemotherapy. One studied starting pemetrexed after a different chemotherapy combination; another studied continuing it after pemetrexed and cisplatin. A separate second-line study found similar survival to docetaxel with fewer important blood-count side effects. These historical comparisons do not predict an individual outcome or describe pemetrexed plus immunotherapy.

clinical.component_rationale: Pemetrexed blocks several enzymes that use folate to make the building blocks of DNA and RNA. This can slow or stop cancer-cell growth. Healthy cells can also be affected. Prescribed folic acid and vitamin B12 reduce important toxicities and are part of treatment.
key_points: NCCP00222a maintenance and 00222b second-line are distinct indications; both exclude predominantly squamous NSCLC.
Pemetrexed 500 mg/m² IV over 10 minutes on Day 1 every 21 days until progression or unacceptable toxicity.
Source v5 replaced nadir-based wording with current-count bands; confirm clinical wellness in borderline continuation rows.
Renal clearance <45 mL/min, haemodialysis and severe hepatic impairment are outside the routine pathway.
Grade 2 first neurotoxicity: hold to baseline then 100% pemetrexed; grade ≥3 or any recurrence: discontinue.
Any grade diarrhoea requiring admission triggers the severe pathway; mucositis and other toxicities have different restart percentages.
No fixed cycle cap or automatic immune-specific monitoring belongs to standalone pemetrexed.

Current product information contraindicates concomitant yellow fever vaccine and advises against other concomitant live attenuated vaccines; retain this as a medicine-information supplement, not an invented NCCP exclusion.

NCCP v5 allows team consideration at ANC 1.0 to <1.5 or platelets 75 to <100 in a clinically well patient; ALIMTA SmPC requires ANC >=1.5 and platelets >=100 before dosing. Reconcile the source difference with consultant/pharmacy; do not treat borderline NCCP rows as automatic clearance.

Assess prior treatment, current benefit, molecular/systemic options and patient priorities.
Exclude hypersensitivity, CrCl <45 and breastfeeding. Pregnancy requires careful specialist necessity and risk assessment under SmPC.
important_cautions: Do not use this standalone assessment for pembrolizumab/pemetrexed maintenance without the combination protocol and immune checks.
NCCP severe hepatic category is not numerically defined; do not invent bilirubin or transaminase cutoffs.
NCCP bleeding footnote uses CTC v2.0 NCI1998; other Table 3 grading edition is unspecified.

support_summary: The source uses folic acid 350–1000 micrograms daily. Take at least five doses in the seven days before the first pemetrexed, continue throughout treatment and for 21 days after the final dose. Follow your own prescription and tell the team about missed doses.

The source uses vitamin B12 1000 micrograms into a muscle during the week before the first pemetrexed, then every three cycles. Later injections may be on treatment day. A change from platinum treatment to maintenance does not automatically restart the B12 clock: your team checks the last dose and the next due date.

Pemetrexed rash prevention uses dexamethasone-equivalent 4 mg twice daily on the day before, day of and day after treatment. Your pharmacist or prescriber should give one clear steroid schedule that also accounts for any anti-sickness medicines. Do not add a second steroid course yourself.

Low emetogenic risk: NCIS V8 reference is ondansetron 8 mg orally on the treatment day and metoclopramide 10 mg orally three times daily as required on subsequent days, with individual suitability and duration confirmed.

At CrCl 45–79, NSAIDs/high-dose aspirin should be avoided 2 days before, treatment day and 2 days after. Long-half-life NSAIDs: at least 5 days before, day of and at least 2 days after; necessary coadministration needs close marrow/GI monitoring. See SmPC 4.5.

rationale.summary: Pemetrexed monotherapy provides a source-listed maintenance or second-line option for selected advanced non-squamous NSCLC. Confirm which treatment context, prior therapy and current alternatives fit the patient.
rationale.setting: Non-squamous NSCLC · standalone maintenance or second-line chemotherapy
rationale.line: Maintenance immediately after platinum chemotherapy without progression, or second-line after prior chemotherapy.
factors: Histology, prior drugs and disease progression status.
Performance status, organ function, toxicity history, patient priorities and current molecular/systemic options.
Vitamin/steroid preparation and medicine-interaction plan.
alternatives: Discuss current disease-specific MDT options, other systemic therapy, trials and supportive care, including not proceeding.
limitations: Maintenance trials selected patients whose disease had not progressed; PARAMOUNT additionally randomised ECOG 0–1 patients after four pemetrexed/cisplatin cycles. NCCP eligibility ECOG 0–2 is broader.
JMEN studied switch maintenance after non-pemetrexed platinum doublets; PARAMOUNT studied continuation. Overall and non-squamous subgroup results and time origins must remain separate.

Hanna2004 enrolled a historical all-histology second-line NSCLC population; its overall survival comparison is not a modern non-squamous subgroup prediction or proof of a pemetrexed survival advantage.
These trials predate modern immunotherapy and many molecular treatments; they do not rank contemporary options or demonstrate pembrolizumab/pemetrexed maintenance benefit.

evidence.trial: JMEN switch maintenance; PARAMOUNT continuation maintenance; Hanna2004 second-line
evidence.population: Three different historical advanced-NSCLC populations; see each endpoint label and limitations.
evidence.comparison: Pemetrexed plus supportive care versus placebo plus supportive care for maintenance; pemetrexed versus docetaxel in second-line treatment.
evidence.applicability: Maintenance studies found longer disease control or survival with pemetrexed than placebo in selected patients whose cancer had not progressed after initial chemotherapy. One studied starting pemetrexed after a different chemotherapy combination; another studied continuing it after pemetrexed and cisplatin. A separate second-line study found similar survival to docetaxel with fewer important blood-count side effects. These historical comparisons do not predict an individual outcome or describe pemetrexed plus immunotherapy.

endpoints.metric: JMEN: overall-trial median OS from maintenance randomisation
endpoints.interpretation: 663 stage IIIB/IV patients without progression after four non-pemetrexed platinum-doublet cycles; includes squamous histology. This is not the non-squamous subgroup result and not survival from induction start.
endpoints.analysis_status: Published trial population result; not an individual prediction

sources.label: JMEN: overall-trial median OS from maintenance randomisation

endpoints.metric: PARAMOUNT: median OS from continuation-maintenance randomisation
endpoints.interpretation: 539 non-progressing advanced non-squamous NSCLC patients with ECOG 0–1 randomised after four pemetrexed/cisplatin cycles; 939 entered induction. Not from first induction dose and not a second-line result.
endpoints.analysis_status: Published trial population result; not an individual prediction

sources.label: PARAMOUNT: median OS from continuation-maintenance randomisation

endpoints.interpretation: 571 previously treated advanced NSCLC patients, ECOG 0–2, after one prior chemotherapy regimen; all-histology study. The OS difference was not statistically significant; do not display as a proven survival gain or a non-squamous-only estimate.
endpoints.analysis_status: Published trial population result; not an individual prediction

sources.label: Hanna2004: overall-trial second-line median OS

limitations: Maintenance trials selected patients whose disease had not progressed; PARAMOUNT additionally randomised ECOG 0–1 patients after four pemetrexed/cisplatin cycles. NCCP eligibility ECOG 0–2 is broader.
JMEN studied switch maintenance after non-pemetrexed platinum doublets; PARAMOUNT studied continuation. Overall and non-squamous subgroup results and time origins must remain separate.

Hanna2004 enrolled a historical all-histology second-line NSCLC population; its overall survival comparison is not a modern non-squamous subgroup prediction or proof of a pemetrexed survival advantage.
These trials predate modern immunotherapy and many molecular treatments; they do not rank contemporary options or demonstrate pembrolizumab/pemetrexed maintenance benefit.
Software source reconciliation is not independent clinical, pharmacy or patient/PPI approval.
evidence.harms: In JMEN, treatment-related grade ≥3 events were more frequent with maintenance pemetrexed than placebo (16% versus 4%). PARAMOUNT reported more grade 3–4 anaemia, fatigue and neutropenia with pemetrexed. Hanna found fewer severe neutropenia and febrile-neutropenia events with pemetrexed than docetaxel. Vitamins do not eliminate toxicity; kidneys, marrow, GI, skin, lung and allergic effects still require review.

Standalone chemotherapy does not imply immune-specific endocrine monitoring; additional immunotherapy requires its matching protocol.
